claim: Primary sensory neurons form the interface between world and brain.
source: Primary sensory neurons form the interface between world and brain.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the role of primary sensory neurons in the nervous system.

claim: The function of primary sensory neurons is well-understood during passive stimulation.
source: Their function is well-understood during passive stimulation but, under natural behaving conditions, sense organs are under active, motor control.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the existing body of literature on passive stimulation studies.

claim: Under natural behaving conditions, sense organs are under active, motor control.
source: Their function is well-understood during passive stimulation but, under natural behaving conditions, sense organs are under active, motor control.
evidence: This is established knowledge about natural sensory behavior.

claim: Primary neuron responses were poorly predicted by whisker angle during active tactile exploration.
source: Using Generalised Linear Models, we found that primary neuron responses were poorly predicted by whisker angle, but well-predicted by rotational forces acting on the whisker: both during touch and free-air whisker motion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from GLM analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Primary neuron responses were well-predicted by rotational forces acting on the whisker during touch.
source: Using Generalised Linear Models, we found that primary neuron responses were poorly predicted by whisker angle, but well-predicted by rotational forces acting on the whisker: both during touch and free-air whisker motion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from GLM analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Primary neuron responses were well-predicted by rotational forces acting on the whisker during free-air whisker motion.
source: Using Generalised Linear Models, we found that primary neuron responses were poorly predicted by whisker angle, but well-predicted by rotational forces acting on the whisker: both during touch and free-air whisker motion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from GLM analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The results are in apparent contrast to previous studies of passive stimulation.
source: These results are in apparent contrast to previous studies of passive stimulation, but could be reconciled by differences in the kinematics-force relationship between active and passive conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cited literature on passive stimulation.

claim: Differences in the kinematics-force relationship between active and passive conditions can reconcile the apparent contrast with previous studies.
source: These results are in apparent contrast to previous studies of passive stimulation, but could be reconciled by differences in the kinematics-force relationship between active and passive conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing active and passive conditions presented in the manuscript.

claim: Simple statistical models can predict rich neural activity elicited by natural, exploratory behaviour involving active movement of sense organs.
source: Thus, simple statistical models can predict rich neural activity elicited by natural, exploratory behaviour involving active movement of sense organs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The active character of sensation, based on motor control of the sense organs, is lost in reduced preparations.
source: However, the active character of sensation (Gibson, 1962; Yarbus, 1967), based on motor control of the sense organs, is lost in reduced preparations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gibson (1962) and Yarbus (1967).

claim: It is now possible to record neuronal activity from an awake mouse, actively exploring the environment with its whiskers, whilst simultaneously measuring whisker kinematics and mechanics.
source: Recent methodological advances permit a way forward: in the whisker system, it is now possible to record neuronal activity from an awake mouse, actively exploring the environment with its whiskers, whilst simultaneously measuring the fundamental sensory variables (whisker kinematics and mechanics) likely to influence neuronal activity (O'Connor et al., 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to O'Connor et al., 2010b.

claim: The manner in which primary neurons encode sensory information fundamentally constrains all downstream neural processing.
source: The manner in which primary neurons encode sensory information fundamentally constrains all downstream neural processing (Lettvin et al., 1959).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lettvin et al., 1959.

claim: PWNs innervate mechanoreceptors located in the whisker follicles.
source: PWNs innervate mechanoreceptors located in the whisker follicles (Zucker and Welker, 1969; Rice et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zucker and Welker, 1969 and Rice et al., 1986.

claim: PWNs are both functionally and morphologically diverse.
source: They are both functionally and morphologically diverse; including types responsive to whisker-object contact and/or whisker self-motion (Szwed et al., 2003; Ebara et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Szwed et al., 2003 and Ebara et al., 2002.

claim: PWNs include types responsive to whisker-object contact and/or whisker self-motion.
source: They are both functionally and morphologically diverse; including types responsive to whisker-object contact and/or whisker self-motion (Szwed et al., 2003; Ebara et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Szwed et al., 2003 and Ebara et al., 2002.

claim: PWNs project to the cerebral cortex via trisynaptic pathways through the brainstem and thalamus.
source: PWNs project to the cerebral cortex, analogously to other modalities, via trisynaptic pathways through the brainstem and thalamus (Diamond et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Diamond et al., 2008.

claim: Moment coding accounts for spiking during both whisker-object interaction and whisker motion in air.
source: Moment coding accounts for spiking during both whisker-object interaction and whisker motion in air.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Moment coding can account for findings in previous studies of passive stimulation in the anaesthetized animal.
source: Moment coding can also account for findings in previous studies of passive stimulation in the anaesthetized animal; indicating that the same biomechanical framework can account for primary somatosensory neuron responses across diverse states.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The same biomechanical framework can account for primary somatosensory neuron responses across diverse states.
source: Moment coding can also account for findings in previous studies of passive stimulation in the anaesthetized animal; indicating that the same biomechanical framework can account for primary somatosensory neuron responses across diverse states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: The results provide a mechanical basis for linking receptor mechanisms to tactile behaviour.
source: Our results provide a mechanical basis for linking receptor mechanisms to tactile behaviour.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: N = 20 units were recorded from awake mice.
source: We recorded the activity of single PWNs from awake mice (Figure 1A,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) as they actively explored a metal pole with their whiskers (N = 20 units).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental sample size.

claim: Whisker motion and whisker shape were recorded using high-speed videography at 1000 frames/s.
source: At the same time, we recorded whisker motion and whisker shape using high-speed videography (1000 frames/s; Figure 1D, Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental methodology.

claim: Each PWN innervates a single whisker follicle.
source: Since each PWN innervates a single whisker follicle, we tracked the 'principal whisker' of each recorded unit from frame to frame, and extracted both the angle and curvature of the principal whisker in each video frame (total 1,496,033 frames; Figure 1B–E; Bale et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PWN anatomy.

claim: A total of 1,496,033 frames were analyzed.
source: Since each PWN innervates a single whisker follicle, we tracked the 'principal whisker' of each recorded unit from frame to frame, and extracted both the angle and curvature of the principal whisker in each video frame (total 1,496,033 frames; Figure 1B–E; Bale et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the amount of data analyzed.

claim: Whiskers are intrinsically curved.
source: Whiskers are intrinsically curved, and the bending moment on a whisker is proportional to how much this curvature changes due to object contact (Birdwell et al., 2007): we therefore used 'curvature change' as a proxy for bending moment (O'Connor et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Birdwell et al., 2007.

claim: The bending moment on a whisker is proportional to how much its curvature changes due to object contact.
source: Whiskers are intrinsically curved, and the bending moment on a whisker is proportional to how much this curvature changes due to object contact (Birdwell et al., 2007): we therefore used 'curvature change' as a proxy for bending moment (O'Connor et al., 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Birdwell et al., 2007 and O'Connor et al., 2010a.

claim: Curvature change was used as a proxy for bending moment.
source: Whiskers are intrinsically curved, and the bending moment on a whisker is proportional to how much this curvature changes due to object contact (Birdwell et al., 2007): we therefore used 'curvature change' as a proxy for bending moment (O'Connor et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is a methodological choice based on cited literature.

claim: Whisker-pole contacts caused substantial whisker bending (curvature change).
source: Whisker-pole contacts caused substantial whisker bending (curvature change), partially correlated with the whisker angle (Figures 1E, 4E) and, consistent with Szwed et al. (2003) and Leiser and Moxon (2007), robust spiking (Figures 1E, 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1E and 4E.

claim: Whisker-pole contacts caused robust spiking, consistent with previous studies.
source: Whisker-pole contacts caused substantial whisker bending (curvature change), partially correlated with the whisker angle (Figures 1E, 4E) and, consistent with Szwed et al. (2003) and Leiser and Moxon (2007), robust spiking (Figures 1E, 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1E and 2E, and citations to Szwed et al. (2003) and Leiser and Moxon (2007).

claim: Curvature change was partially correlated with whisker angle during whisker-pole contacts.
source: Whisker-pole contacts caused substantial whisker bending (curvature change), partially correlated with the whisker angle (Figures 1E, 4E) and, consistent with Szwed et al. (2003) and Leiser and Moxon (2007), robust spiking (Figures 1E, 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1E and 4E.

claim: GLMs driven by whisker angle have previously been shown to provide a simple but accurate description of the response of PWNs to passive stimulation.
source: GLMs, driven by whisker angle, have previously been shown to provide a simple but accurate description of the response of PWNs to passive stimulation (Bale et al., 2013) and have mathematical properties ideal for robust parameter-fitting (Truccolo et al., 2005; Paninski et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bale et al., 2013.

claim: GLMs have mathematical properties ideal for robust parameter-fitting.
source: GLMs, driven by whisker angle, have previously been shown to provide a simple but accurate description of the response of PWNs to passive stimulation (Bale et al., 2013) and have mathematical properties ideal for robust parameter-fitting (Truccolo et al., 2005; Paninski et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Truccolo et al., 2005 and Paninski et al., 2007.

claim: The median number of frames per unit was 69,672.
source: For each recorded unit (median 69,672 frames and 550 spikes per unit), we computed the GLM parameters that best predicted the unit's spike train given the whisker angle time series, using half the data as a training set for parameter-fitting (8 total fitted parameters - 5 for stimulus filter, 2 for history filter, 1 bias; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data characteristics.

claim: The median number of spikes per unit was 550.
source: For each recorded unit (median 69,672 frames and 550 spikes per unit), we computed the GLM parameters that best predicted the unit's spike train given the whisker angle time series, using half the data as a training set for parameter-fitting (8 total fitted parameters - 5 for stimulus filter, 2 for history filter, 1 bias; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data characteristics.

claim: 8 total parameters were fitted for the GLM (5 for stimulus filter, 2 for history filter, 1 bias).
source: For each recorded unit (median 69,672 frames and 550 spikes per unit), we computed the GLM parameters that best predicted the unit's spike train given the whisker angle time series, using half the data as a training set for parameter-fitting (8 total fitted parameters - 5 for stimulus filter, 2 for history filter, 1 bias; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methodological approach.

claim: Angle GLMs predicted spike trains of only 2/20 units moderately well (PCC > 0.5).
source: Although angle GLMs predicted spike trains of a few units moderately well (2/20 units had PCC > 0.5), they performed poorly for the majority (median PCC 0.06, IQR 0.019–0.3; Figure 2B–D, orange).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Angle GLMs performed poorly for the majority of units (median PCC 0.06, IQR 0.019–0.3).
source: Although angle GLMs predicted spike trains of a few units moderately well (2/20 units had PCC > 0.5), they performed poorly for the majority (median PCC 0.06, IQR 0.019–0.3; Figure 2B–D, orange).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Quadratic GLMs fared only marginally better than linear angle GLMs (median PCC 0.097, IQR 0.042–0.31; p=0.044).
source: This was unlikely to be because of non-linear tuning to whisker angle, since quadratic GLMs fared only marginally better (median PCC 0.097, IQR 0.042–0.31; p=0.044, signed-rank test, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Curvature GLMs were substantially more accurate than angle GLMs at the population level (median PCC 0.52, IQR 0.22–0.66; p=0.0044).
source: In contrast, we found that, at the population level, the curvature GLMs were substantially more accurate than the angle GLMs (median PCC 0.52, IQR 0.22–0.66; p=0.0044, signed-rank test; Figure 2B–D, blue) with prediction accuracy up to PCC 0.88.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Curvature GLM prediction accuracy reached up to PCC 0.88.
source: In contrast, we found that, at the population level, the curvature GLMs were substantially more accurate than the angle GLMs (median PCC 0.52, IQR 0.22–0.66; p=0.0044, signed-rank test; Figure 2B–D, blue) with prediction accuracy up to PCC 0.88.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Curvature GLMs predicted spikes during touch episodes significantly more accurately (median PCC 0.57, IQR 0.23–0.72) than angle GLMs during non-touch episodes (median 0.06, IQR 0.02–0.35; p=0.005).
source: Curvature GLMs also predicted spikes during touch episodes significantly more accurately (median PCC 0.57, IQR 0.23–0.72) than did angle GLMs during non-touch episodes (median 0.06, IQR 0.02–0.35; p=0.005, signed-rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing touch and non-touch episodes.

claim: 90% of units had above chance PCC and were termed 'curvature-sensitive'.
source: At the level of individual units, 90% had above chance PCC and we termed these 'curvature-sensitive' (Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Of the curvature-sensitive units, 61% were sensitive to positive curvature change and 39% to negative curvature change.
source: Of the curvature-sensitive units, 61% were sensitive to positive curvature change and 39% to negative curvature change (Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the experimental data.

claim: A GLM sensitive to instantaneous curvature (4 parameters) exhibited very similar prediction accuracy to the full GLM.
source: The result that curvature predicted PWN responses better than angle was robust to the number of fitted parameters: a GLM sensitive to instantaneous curvature (4 parameters: 1 stimulus filter parameter, 2 history filter parameters and 1 bias) exhibited very similar prediction accuracy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Prediction accuracy based on curvature was significantly greater than that based on angle for smoothing time-scales in the range 1–100 ms (p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected).
source: The result was also robust to time-scale: prediction accuracy based on curvature was significantly greater than that based on angle for smoothing time-scales in the range 1–100 ms (signed-rank test, p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: When a mouse whisks against an object, curvature change and angle fluctuate in concert.
source: When a mouse whisks against an object, curvature change and angle fluctuate in concert (Birdwell et al., 2007; Bagdasarian et al., 2013; Pammer et al., 2013; Figures 1E, 4E and Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and data shown in Figures 1E, 4E, 4F-G.

claim: GLMs using both curvature change and angle as input predicted spike trains no more accurately (median PCC 0.53, IQR 0.40–0.62; p=0.067) than GLMs based on curvature change alone.
source: When we fitted GLMs using both curvature change and angle as input, these GLMs predicted the spike trains no more accurately (median PCC 0.53, IQR 0.40–0.62; p=0.067, signed-rank test; Figure 2D) than GLMs based on curvature change alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: For 65% of units, curvature change GLMs predicted spikes better than angle (p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected).
source: Moreover, on a unit-by-unit basis, for 65% of units, curvature change GLMs predicted spikes better than angle (signed-rank test, p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected); only for 5% of units did angle predict spikes better than curvature change.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: For only 5% of units did angle predict spikes better than curvature change.
source: Moreover, on a unit-by-unit basis, for 65% of units, curvature change GLMs predicted spikes better than angle (signed-rank test, p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected); only for 5% of units did angle predict spikes better than curvature change.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: GLMs based on curvature change predicted spike trains more accurately than GLMs based on 'push angle' (median PCC 0.25, IQR 0.04–0.45; p=0.006).
source: GLMs based on curvature change also predicted spike trains more accurately than GLMs based on 'push angle' – the change in angle as the whisker pushes against an object (Figure 1E; median PCC 0.25, IQR 0.04–0.45; p=0.006, signed-rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Prediction accuracy of GLMs fitted with both push angle and curvature change inputs (median PCC 0.52, IQR 0.2–0.69) was no better than that of GLMs fitted with curvature alone (p=0.43).
source: Moreover, prediction accuracy of GLMs fitted with both push angle and curvature change (median PCC 0.52, IQR 0.2–0.69) inputs was no better than that of GLMs fitted with curvature alone (p=0.43, signed-rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Under the experimental conditions, axial/lateral force components were near-perfectly correlated with bending moment.
source: We restricted our analysis to bending moment since, under our experimental conditions, axial/lateral force components were near-perfectly correlated with bending moment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and bending moment is likely to have a major influence on stresses in the follicle (Pammer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bending moment is likely to have a major influence on stresses in the follicle.
source: We restricted our analysis to bending moment since, under our experimental conditions, axial/lateral force components were near-perfectly correlated with bending moment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and bending moment is likely to have a major influence on stresses in the follicle (Pammer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pammer et al., 2013.

claim: Units fired at a higher rate during touch than otherwise.
source: Units fired at a higher rate during touch than otherwise (Szwed et al., 2003; Leiser and Moxon, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Szwed et al., 2003 and Leiser and Moxon, 2007.

claim: Curvature-based GLMs reproduced the effect of higher firing rate during touch without any further parameter-adjustment.
source: Without any further parameter-adjustment, the curvature-based GLMs reproduced this effect (Figure 2E): the correlation coefficient between recorded and GLM-predicted firing rate for touch episodes was 0.97.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: The correlation coefficient between recorded and GLM-predicted firing rate for touch episodes was 0.97.
source: Without any further parameter-adjustment, the curvature-based GLMs reproduced this effect (Figure 2E): the correlation coefficient between recorded and GLM-predicted firing rate for touch episodes was 0.97.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: During free whisking, whisker curvature changed little.
source: During free whisking - in the absence of whisker-pole contact - whisker curvature, and therefore bending moment, changed little (Figure 1E, Figure 4F); consistent with previous studies (Knutsen et al., 2008; Quist et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1E and 4F, and citations to Knutsen et al., 2008 and Quist et al., 2014.

claim: 50% of recorded units were significantly modulated by whisking amplitude.
source: Yet, 50% of recorded units ('whisking-sensitive units') were significantly modulated by whisking amplitude (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: 45% of PWNs were curvature-sensitive but not whisking-sensitive.
source: Consistent with Szwed et al. (2003), PWNs were diverse: 45% were curvature-sensitive (significant PCC for curvature based GLM) but not whisking-sensitive; 45% were both curvature- and whisking-sensitive; 5% were whisking-sensitive but not curvature-sensitive.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the experimental data and citation to Szwed et al. (2003).

claim: 45% of PWNs were both curvature- and whisking-sensitive.
source: Consistent with Szwed et al. (2003), PWNs were diverse: 45% were curvature-sensitive (significant PCC for curvature based GLM) but not whisking-sensitive; 45% were both curvature- and whisking-sensitive; 5% were whisking-sensitive but not curvature-sensitive.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the experimental data and citation to Szwed et al. (2003).

claim: 5% of PWNs were whisking-sensitive but not curvature-sensitive.
source: Consistent with Szwed et al. (2003), PWNs were diverse: 45% were curvature-sensitive (significant PCC for curvature based GLM) but not whisking-sensitive; 45% were both curvature- and whisking-sensitive; 5% were whisking-sensitive but not curvature-sensitive.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the experimental data and citation to Szwed et al. (2003).

claim: The moment associated with the rotational acceleration of a whisker is proportional to the whisker's angular acceleration.
source: A likely candidate is the moment associated with the rotational acceleration of a whisker: this moment is proportional to the whisker's angular acceleration (Quist et al., 2014; Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Quist et al., 2014.

claim: Whisking-sensitive units were tuned to angular acceleration.
source: Consistent with this possibility, we found that whisking-sensitive units were tuned to angular acceleration (Figure 3B) and that 50% of these were phase-modulated (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: 50% of whisking-sensitive units were phase-modulated.
source: Consistent with this possibility, we found that whisking-sensitive units were tuned to angular acceleration (Figure 3B) and that 50% of these were phase-modulated (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Angular acceleration tuning was diverse: some units fired to acceleration in a particular direction (rostral or caudal), whilst others responded to acceleration in both directions.
source: Angular acceleration tuning was diverse: some units fired to acceleration in a particular direction (rostral or caudal), whilst others responded to acceleration in both directions (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For whisking-sensitive units, quadratic GLMs trained on non-touch episodes were able to predict spikes using whisker angle acceleration as input (median PCC 0.37, IQR 0.18–0.58).
source: Moreover, for whisking-sensitive units (but not whisking-insensitive ones), quadratic GLMs trained on data from non-touch episodes were able to predict spikes using whisker angle acceleration as input (Figure 3D–E; whisking-sensitive units, median PCC 0.37, IQR 0.18–0.58; whisking-insensitive, median PCC -0.0071, IQR -0.035–0.041; p=0.0017 rank-sum test for whisking-sensitive vs whisking-insensitive units).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3D-E.

claim: For whisking-insensitive units, quadratic GLMs trained on non-touch episodes had poor prediction performance (median PCC -0.0071, IQR -0.035–0.041).
source: Moreover, for whisking-sensitive units (but not whisking-insensitive ones), quadratic GLMs trained on data from non-touch episodes were able to predict spikes using whisker angle acceleration as input (Figure 3D–E; whisking-sensitive units, median PCC 0.37, IQR 0.18–0.58; whisking-insensitive, median PCC -0.0071, IQR -0.035–0.041; p=0.0017 rank-sum test for whisking-sensitive vs whisking-insensitive units).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3D-E.

claim: The difference in prediction performance between whisking-sensitive and whisking-insensitive units was statistically significant (p=0.0017, rank-sum test).
source: Moreover, for whisking-sensitive units (but not whisking-insensitive ones), quadratic GLMs trained on data from non-touch episodes were able to predict spikes using whisker angle acceleration as input (Figure 3D–E; whisking-sensitive units, median PCC 0.37, IQR 0.18–0.58; whisking-insensitive, median PCC -0.0071, IQR -0.035–0.041; p=0.0017 rank-sum test for whisking-sensitive vs whisking-insensitive units).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: For 70% of whisking-sensitive units, directional selectivity for acceleration was consistent with that for curvature.
source: For 70% of whisking-sensitive units, directional selectivity for acceleration was consistent with that for curvature.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the experimental data.

claim: In the absence of whisker-object contact, responses of PWNs to whisking itself can be accounted for by sensitivity to the moment associated with angular whisker acceleration.
source: These findings indicate that, in the absence of whisker-object contact, responses of PWNs to whisking itself can be accounted for by sensitivity to the moment associated with angular whisker acceleration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data on whisking-sensitive units.

claim: Studies using passive whisker stimulation have reported that PWNs encode whisker angle and its temporal derivatives.
source: In apparent contrast, studies using passive whisker stimulation have reported that PWNs encode whisker angle and its temporal derivatives (Zucker and Welker, 1969; Gibson and Welker, 1983; Lichtenstein et al., 1990; Jones et al., 2004; Arabzadeh et al., 2005; Bale and Petersen, 2009; Lottem and Azouz, 2011; Bale et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: During active pole exploration, angle and curvature change were only loosely related (median correlation coefficient 0.20, IQR 0.079–0.39).
source: During active pole exploration, angle and curvature change were, over all, only loosely related (median correlation coefficient 0.20, IQR 0.079–0.39, Figures 4D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 4D-E.

claim: The angle-curvature relationship was different for touch compared to non-touch.
source: Important contributory factors were that the angle-curvature relationship was both different for touch compared to non-touch (Figure 4F) and dependent on object location (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: The angle-curvature relationship was dependent on object location.
source: Important contributory factors were that the angle-curvature relationship was both different for touch compared to non-touch (Figure 4F) and dependent on object location (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4G.

claim: During passive stimulation, whisker angle was near perfectly correlated with curvature change (for C2, correlation coefficients 0.96 and 0.94 respectively).
source: In contrast, during passive stimulation, whisker angle was near perfectly correlated with curvature change (for C2, correlation coefficients 0.96 and 0.94 respectively; similar results for C5; Figures 4C–D, Figure 4E, inset and Figure 4—figure supplement 2); consistent with properties of cantilevered beams (Birdwell et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 4C-D, Figure 4E inset, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The near perfect correlation between angle and curvature during passive stimulation is consistent with properties of cantilevered beams.
source: In contrast, during passive stimulation, whisker angle was near perfectly correlated with curvature change (for C2, correlation coefficients 0.96 and 0.94 respectively; similar results for C5; Figures 4C–D, Figure 4E, inset and Figure 4—figure supplement 2); consistent with properties of cantilevered beams (Birdwell et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Birdwell et al., 2007.

claim: Simulations confirmed that, due to the tight relationship between angle and curvature during passive stimulation, a unit tuned purely to curvature change can appear tightly tuned to angle.
source: Simulations confirmed that, due to the tight relationship between the variables, a unit tuned purely to curvature change can appear tightly tuned to angle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Apparent sensitivity to whisker angle under passive stimulation conditions can be accounted for by moment-tuning.
source: The implication is that apparent sensitivity to whisker angle under passive stimulation conditions can be accounted for by moment-tuning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results and experimental data.

claim: Theories of sensory encoding suggest that neural circuits have evolved to operate efficiently under natural conditions.
source: Theories of sensory encoding suggest that neural circuits have evolved to operate efficiently under natural conditions (Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001; Reinagel, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001 and Reinagel, 2001.

claim: Previous studies have succeeded in predicting/decoding spikes evoked by passive presentation of natural sensory stimuli to anaesthetised/immobilised animals.
source: Previous studies have succeeded in predicting/decoding spikes evoked by passive presentation of natural sensory stimuli to anaesthetised/immobilised animals (Lewen et al., 2001; Arabzadeh et al., 2005; Pillow et al., 2008; Mante et al., 2008; Lottem and Azouz, 2011; Bale et al., 2013), but it has been difficult to extend this approach to encompass natural, active movement of the sense organs.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: It has been difficult to extend the spike prediction approach to encompass natural, active movement of the sense organs.
source: Previous studies have succeeded in predicting/decoding spikes evoked by passive presentation of natural sensory stimuli to anaesthetised/immobilised animals (Lewen et al., 2001; Arabzadeh et al., 2005; Pillow et al., 2008; Mante et al., 2008; Lottem and Azouz, 2011; Bale et al., 2013), but it has been difficult to extend this approach to encompass natural, active movement of the sense organs.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous research approaches.

claim: Model prediction correlation coefficients reached up to 0.88.
source: Given that, for each unit, we were attempting to predict the entire ~70 s time course of activity, the variability of the behaviour of untrained mice (O'Connor et al., 2010a), and the lack of trial-averaging as a noise reduction strategy, it is remarkable that we found model prediction correlation coefficients up to 0.88.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claim: A valuable feature of the GLM training procedure is that it takes correlations between sensory variables into account.
source: A challenge of studying neural coding under unconstrained, awake conditions is that sensory variables tend to correlate. A valuable feature of the GLM training procedure is that it takes such correlations into account.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological properties of GLMs.

claim: Although whisker angle predicted spikes for a subset of units, this effect was very largely explained by a curvature-coding model, together with the correlation between angle and curvature.
source: We found that, although whisker angle predicted spikes for a subset of units, this effect was very largely explained by a curvature-coding model, together with the correlation between angle and curvature.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and GLM analysis.

claim: Pushing a whisker against an object triggers spiking in many PWNs.
source: Pushing a whisker against an object triggers spiking in many PWNs (Szwed et al., 2003; Szwed et al., 2006; Leiser and Moxon, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Szwed et al., 2003, Szwed et al., 2006, and Leiser and Moxon, 2007.

claim: Biomechanical modelling by Hartmann and co-workers accounts for PWN spiking by a framework where the whisker is idealised as an elastic beam, cantilever-mounted in the skin.
source: Biomechanical modelling by Hartmann and co-workers accounts for this by a framework where the whisker is idealised as an elastic beam, cantilever-mounted in the skin (Birdwell et al., 2007; Quist et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Birdwell et al., 2007 and Quist et al., 2014.

claim: When an elastic beam pushes against an object, the beam bends, causing reaction forces at its base.
source: When such a beam pushes against an object, the beam bends, causing reaction forces at its base.
evidence: This is a statement of biomechanical principles.

claim: The data are in striking agreement with the general suggestion that mechanoreceptor activity is closely related to reaction forces at the whisker base.
source: Our data are in striking agreement with the general suggestion that mechanoreceptor activity is closely related to such reaction forces.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Curvature change associated with contact-induced whisker bending predicts PWN spiking.
source: Our results show that curvature change associated with contact-induced whisker bending, and acceleration associated with whisker rotation, predict PWN spiking.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental findings.

claim: Acceleration associated with whisker rotation predicts PWN spiking.
source: Our results show that curvature change associated with contact-induced whisker bending, and acceleration associated with whisker rotation, predict PWN spiking.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental findings.

claim: The results provide a mechanical basis for previous findings of 'touch' and 'whisking-touch' units.
source: Our results also provide a mechanical basis for previous findings: our finding of subtypes of curvature-only and curvature-acceleration PWNs is consistent with previous reports of 'touch' and 'whisking-touch' units (Szwed et al., 2003; 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: A common framework accounts for diverse PWN properties.
source: Thus, a common framework accounts for diverse PWN properties.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The finding that whisker angle predicts PWN spikes poorly indicates that whisker angle can change without modulating mechanotransduction in the follicle.
source: Our finding that whisker angle predicts PWN spikes poorly indicates that whisker angle can change without modulating mechanotransduction in the follicle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: During artificial whisking, the follicle-shaft complex moves as a rigid unit.
source: This is consistent with evidence that, during artificial whisking, the follicle-shaft complex moves as a rigid unit (Bagdasarian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bagdasarian et al., 2013.

claim: Previous studies using passive stimulation in anaesthetised animals have consistently reported a tight relationship between whisker kinematics and PWN response.
source: In apparent contrast, previous studies using passive stimulation in anaesthetised animals have consistently reported a tight relationship between whisker kinematics and PWN response.
evidence: This is a statement about the findings of previous research.

claim: In the cantilever whisker model, passively induced changes in whisker angle correlate highly with whisker bending.
source: In the cantilever whisker model, passively induced changes in whisker angle correlate highly with whisker bending.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the cantilever whisker model.

claim: The study confirmed that the cantilever model applies to real whiskers in vivo.
source: We confirmed that this applies to real whiskers in vivo and demonstrate that moment-sensitive units can thereby appear angle-tuned.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental findings.

claim: Moment-sensitive units can appear angle-tuned during passive stimulation.
source: We confirmed that this applies to real whiskers in vivo and demonstrate that moment-sensitive units can thereby appear angle-tuned.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and simulations.

claim: Moment-encoding can account for primary neuron responses not only during active touch but also under passive stimulation.
source: In this way, moment-encoding can account for primary neuron responses not only during active touch but also under passive stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The results highlight the importance of studying neurons under natural, active sensing conditions.
source: More generally, our results highlight the importance of studying neurons under natural, active sensing conditions.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Pole contact is well-suited to reaction force estimation.
source: In this study, we considered PWN encoding under conditions of pole contact, since this is well-suited to reaction force estimation (O'Connor et al., 2010a; Pammer et al., 2013) and involves object-stimulus interactions on a ~100 ms time-scale that is conducive to single-trial analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Connor et al., 2010a and Pammer et al., 2013.

claim: Pole contact involves object-stimulus interactions on a ~100 ms time-scale that is conducive to single-trial analysis.
source: In this study, we considered PWN encoding under conditions of pole contact, since this is well-suited to reaction force estimation (O'Connor et al., 2010a; Pammer et al., 2013) and involves object-stimulus interactions on a ~100 ms time-scale that is conducive to single-trial analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design rationale.

claim: Since whisker bending is ubiquitous in whisking behaviour, it is likely that the finding of curvature sensitivity is a general one.
source: Since whisker bending is ubiquitous in whisking behaviour, it is likely that our finding of curvature sensitivity is a general one.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Prediction performance varied across units, suggesting that other force components may also be encoded.
source: However, prediction performance varied across units, suggesting that other force components may also be encoded.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the variability in the experimental data.

claim: Other experimental conditions may involve multiple force components and/or encoding of information by spike timing on a finer time-scale.
source: Other experimental conditions – for example, textured surfaces – may involve multiple force components (Quist and Hartmann, 2012; Pammer et al., 2013; Bagdasarian et al., 2013) and/or encoding of information by spike timing on a finer time-scale (Panzeri et al., 2001; Petersen et al., 2001; Arabzadeh et al., 2005; Bale et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is axiomatic that mechanoreceptors are sensors of internal forces acting in the tissue within which they are embedded.
source: It is axiomatic that mechanoreceptors are sensors of internal forces acting in the tissue within which they are embedded (Abraira and Ginty, 2013) and therefore valuable to be able to measure mechanical forces in the awake, behaving animal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Abraira and Ginty, 2013.

claim: In the case of primate hand-use, the complex biomechanics of skin makes force-estimation difficult.
source: In general, including the important case of primate hand-use, the complex biomechanics of skin makes force-estimation difficult (Phillips and Johnson, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Phillips and Johnson, 1981.

claim: For whiskers, the quasi-static relationship between bending moment and curvature is relatively simple: the bending moment on a whisker is proportional to its curvature.
source: In contrast, for whiskers, the quasi-static relationship is relatively simple: the bending moment on a whisker is proportional to its curvature.
evidence: This is a statement of biomechanical principles specific to whiskers.

claim: Reaction forces can be directly estimated from videography in vivo for whiskers.
source: This has the important implication that reaction forces can be directly estimated from videography in vivo (Birdwell et al., 2007; O'Connor et al., 2010a; Pammer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Birdwell et al., 2007, O'Connor et al., 2010a, and Pammer et al., 2013.

claim: The results are the first direct demonstration that reaction forces drive primary sensory neuron responses.
source: Our results are the first direct demonstration that such reaction forces drive primary sensory neuron responses – likely involving Piezo2 ion channels (Woo et al., 2014; Poole et al., 2015; Whiteley et al., 2015) – and provide insight into how sensitivity to touch and self-motion arises in the somatosensory pathway (Szwed et al., 2003; Yu et al., 2006; Curtis and Kleinfeld, 2009; Khatri et al., 2009; O'Connor et al., 2010b; Huber et al., 2012; Petreanu et al., 2012; Peron et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Reaction forces likely involve Piezo2 ion channels.
source: Our results are the first direct demonstration that such reaction forces drive primary sensory neuron responses – likely involving Piezo2 ion channels (Woo et al., 2014; Poole et al., 2015; Whiteley et al., 2015) – and provide insight into how sensitivity to touch and self-motion arises in the somatosensory pathway (Szwed et al., 2003; Yu et al., 2006; Curtis and Kleinfeld, 2009; Khatri et al., 2009; O'Connor et al., 2010b; Huber et al., 2012; Petreanu et al., 2012; Peron et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Woo et al., 2014, Poole et al., 2015, and Whiteley et al., 2015.

claim: The results provide insight into how sensitivity to touch and self-motion arises in the somatosensory pathway.
source: Our results are the first direct demonstration that such reaction forces drive primary sensory neuron responses – likely involving Piezo2 ion channels (Woo et al., 2014; Poole et al., 2015; Whiteley et al., 2015) – and provide insight into how sensitivity to touch and self-motion arises in the somatosensory pathway (Szwed et al., 2003; Yu et al., 2006; Curtis and Kleinfeld, 2009; Khatri et al., 2009; O'Connor et al., 2010b; Huber et al., 2012; Petreanu et al., 2012; Peron et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by multiple citations.

claim: Extraction of bending moment is a useful first step for many tactile computations.
source: Extraction of bending moment is a useful first step for many tactile computations.
evidence: This is a general statement about the computational significance of the findings.

claim: Large transients in bending moment signal object-touch events.
source: Large transients in bending moment signal object-touch events, and the magnitude of bending is inversely proportional to the radial distance of contact along the whisker (Solomon and Hartmann, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Solomon and Hartmann, 2006.

claim: The magnitude of bending is inversely proportional to the radial distance of contact along the whisker.
source: Large transients in bending moment signal object-touch events, and the magnitude of bending is inversely proportional to the radial distance of contact along the whisker (Solomon and Hartmann, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Solomon and Hartmann, 2006.

claim: If integrated with cues for whisker self-motion, whisker bending can be a cue to the 3D location of an object.
source: As illustrated by our results on the statistics of active touch, if integrated with cues for whisker self-motion, whisker bending can be a cue to the 3D location of an object (Szwed et al., 2003; 2006; Birdwell et al., 2007; Bagdasarian et al., 2013; Pammer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and the experimental results.

claim: Bending moment can permit wall following.
source: Bending moment can permit wall following (Sofroniew et al., 2014) and, if integrated across whiskers, can in principle be used both to infer object shape (Solomon and Hartmann, 2006) and to map the spatial structure of the environment (Fox et al., 2012; Pearson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sofroniew et al., 2014.

claim: If integrated across whiskers, bending moment can in principle be used to infer object shape.
source: Bending moment can permit wall following (Sofroniew et al., 2014) and, if integrated across whiskers, can in principle be used both to infer object shape (Solomon and Hartmann, 2006) and to map the spatial structure of the environment (Fox et al., 2012; Pearson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Solomon and Hartmann, 2006.

claim: If integrated across whiskers, bending moment can in principle be used to map the spatial structure of the environment.
source: Bending moment can permit wall following (Sofroniew et al., 2014) and, if integrated across whiskers, can in principle be used both to infer object shape (Solomon and Hartmann, 2006) and to map the spatial structure of the environment (Fox et al., 2012; Pearson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fox et al., 2012 and Pearson et al., 2013.

claim: The responses of primary whisker neurons can be predicted, during natural behaviour that includes active motor control of the sense organ, from forces acting on the whiskers.
source: We have shown that the responses of primary whisker neurons can be predicted, during natural behaviour that includes active motor control of the sense organ, from forces acting on the whiskers.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: The results provide a bridge linking receptor mechanisms to behaviour.
source: These results provide a bridge linking receptor mechanisms to behaviour.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the significance of the findings.

claim: All experimental protocols were approved by both United Kingdom Home Office national authorities and institutional ethical review.
source: All experimental protocols were approved by both United Kingdom Home Office national authorities and institutional ethical review.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Mice used in the study were C57 strain, N=10, 6 weeks at time of implant.
source: Mice (C57; N=10; 6 weeks at time of implant) were anesthetized with isoflurane (2% by volume in O2), mounted in a stereotaxic apparatus (Narishige, London, UK) and body temperature maintained at 37°C using a homeothermic heating system.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental subjects and procedures.

claim: Moment was highly linearly correlated with lateral force (median absolute correlation coefficient across units 0.995, IQR 0.99–1.00, median R2 of linear fit 0.99, IQR 0.97–1.00).
source: Moment was highly linearly correlated with lateral force (median absolute correlation coefficient across units 0.995, IQR 0.99–1.00, median R2 of linear fit 0.99, IQR 0.97–1.00), and highly quadratically correlated with axial force (median R2 of quadratic fit 0.94, IQR 0.85–0.98).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Moment was highly quadratically correlated with axial force (median R2 of quadratic fit 0.94, IQR 0.85–0.98).
source: Moment was highly linearly correlated with lateral force (median absolute correlation coefficient across units 0.995, IQR 0.99–1.00, median R2 of linear fit 0.99, IQR 0.97–1.00), and highly quadratically correlated with axial force (median R2 of quadratic fit 0.94, IQR 0.85–0.98).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under the experimental conditions of pole exploration, axial force and lateral force are both redundant with moment.
source: This indicates that, during our conditions of pole exploration, axial force and lateral force are both redundant with moment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation data.
